questions: Do you have difficulty voluntarily looking up or down?
Is looking downward more difficult than looking upward?
Can your eyes move up or down normally when your head is moved for you?
Did repeated falls, especially backward, begin within the first three years of your other symptoms?
Do you have stiffness or slowness mainly in your neck and trunk rather than in your limbs?
Have your movements failed to improve substantially with levodopa or other Parkinson’s medications?
Do you have trouble initiating walking or feel as if your feet are stuck to the floor?
Have you developed unusually rapid changes in thinking, personality, judgment, or motivation?
Do you have difficulty voluntarily opening your eyelids or episodes when your eyelids clamp shut?
Do you have slurred speech or difficulty swallowing?
Do you have a prominent tremor when your limbs are at rest?
Have you had marked dizziness on standing, urinary retention, or loss of bladder control early in the illness?
Have you experienced well-formed visual hallucinations?
Do you act out your dreams during sleep?
Is one limb much more affected than the other, with difficulty performing learned movements despite preserved strength?
Have you had episodes of weakness, numbness, or sudden worsening suggestive of strokes?
Do you have prominent limb or gait incoordination that is worse than your stiffness or slowness?

results: 1. Comprehensive neuro-ophthalmologic examination, including saccades, pursuit, vestibulo-ocular reflexes, convergence, pupils, ptosis, and fatigability
bedside eye-movement exam: vertical gaze palsy progressing to complete external ophthalmoplegia
cranial nerve examination: vertical gaze palsy progressing to complete external ophthalmoplegia
2. Bedside examination for cerebellar, sensory, vestibular, pyramidal, extrapyramidal, and frontal gait abnormalities
Romberg test: negative - swaying is not worse with the eyes closed
deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses: normal
3. MRI of the brain with thin-section views through the midbrain, pons, cerebellum, basal ganglia, and orbits
brain MRI: no structural lesion accounting for the syndrome
acetylcholine receptor, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies: normal
5. Serum creatine kinase, thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, vitamin B12, vitamin E, copper, and ceruloplasmin
copper / caeruloplasmin: normal - excludes Wilson disease
6. Nerve conduction studies and repetitive nerve stimulation with single-fiber EMG
8. Genetic testing for mitochondrial disease and spinocerebellar ataxia/oculomotor syndromes
genetic ataxia panel: no pathogenic repeat expansion or variant
9. Cerebrospinal-fluid examination with cell count, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands, autoimmune encephalitis antibodies, and paraneoplastic antibodies
lumbar puncture / CSF: normal cells, protein and glucose; no oligoclonal bands
CSF cell count and differential: normal
CSF oligoclonal bands and IgG index: normal
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Mitochondrial progressive external ophthalmoplegia with cerebellar ataxia, most likely due to a mitochondrial DNA maintenance disorder (POLG or TWNK-related disease)

ALTERNATIVE: Niemann–Pick disease type C

ALTERNATIVE: Progressive supranuclear palsy (4-repeat tauopathy)

ALTERNATIVE: Anti-GQ1b antibody syndrome (Miller Fisher/Bickerstaff spectrum)
